problem_shape: This family is about deciding what can be trusted when digital evidence is easy to copy, edit, generate, or present out of context. The real-world object may be a micro-video, a vaccine image, a sustainability claim, a scientific citation, a chatbot correction, a Community Note, an autonomous-driving simulation, a feedback label, or a security-camera stream. In every case, the system is not merely asking whether a piece of content looks plausible. It is asking where the claim came from, what evidence supports it, who checked it, whether private data can stay hidden, and whether the final confidence is deserved. The shared pressure is that trust now depends on a chain: source, content, context, retrieval, human judgment, model judgment, and sometimes cryptographic proof. A weak link can make a true-looking answer unsafe. These papers belong together because they treat misinformation and trust as evidence-management problems. They try to gather the right clues, compare them to reliable references, expose why a judgment was made, and prevent users or models from mistaking fluent presentation for verified truth.
naive_failure: A smart beginner would first build a classifier that labels content true or false, perhaps with a bigger language or vision model and a list of known bad examples. That fails because misinformation is not one stable visual or textual pattern. It can be a real image paired with the wrong event, a persuasive professional-looking fact-check, a video edited in small ways, a generated reference, a green claim that omits key context, or a crowd rating that changes after public display. Another simple idea is to retrieve evidence and trust whatever appears most similar. That fails when retrieved evidence is incomplete, irrelevant, manipulated, private, or too costly to check at scale. A third shortcut is to show a confidence score, but confidence can be overblown when the model has weak evidence. Across the family, the naive failure is treating trust as a single label rather than a chain of claims that must be inspected.
mathematical_principle: The recurring mathematical idea is controlled comparison under uncertainty. Each paper starts by turning a messy trust question into smaller things that can be checked: a video frame against external evidence, a claim against a knowledge source, a citation against a repository, a user rating before and after display, a private feedback label against a proof rule, or a model answer against signals of internal stability. The math then asks which comparisons should count and how much confidence they deserve. Retrieval methods measure closeness between a claim and possible evidence, while accepting that closeness is only a clue, not proof. Ranking methods choose which evidence or explanation should be inspected first. Time-series methods compare behavior before and after an event, such as a Community Note being shown, to see whether public display changes agreement. Privacy and verification methods add carefully designed checks: a party can prove that a rule was followed or noise was added without revealing the underlying private data. The common tradeoff is evidence versus exposure: the system needs enough signal to judge trust, while hiding sensitive data, saving effort, and avoiding false certainty.
why_math_matters: The math matters because trust has structure that ordinary rules cannot handle. Evidence is often scattered across text, images, videos, graphs, databases, people, and time. A rule such as \"look for suspicious words\" misses out-of-context media, visual vaccine claims, fake scholarly references, and sustainability statements whose problem is omission rather than an obvious lie. A rule such as \"trust the crowd\" misses polarization and instability, as shown by work on Community Notes. A rule such as \"trust the retrieved source\" misses the fact that a generated answer can sound certain while the useful subgraph or repository match is incomplete. These papers use comparison, aggregation, calibration, proof, and sequence tracking because the world gives repeated partial clues, not perfect labels. Multimodal systems combine what is seen, said, and retrieved. Agent systems split the checking task across roles so weak clues do not drown out anomalies. Verification systems use public checks and hidden data together. The math is the language for balancing useful evidence, privacy, speed, and warranted confidence.
paper_family: The representative papers are siblings because they all repair a broken trust chain at different points. FakeAgent and TrueLens focus on video: they gather visual and outside evidence so a micro-video or fake-news clip is not judged by surface appearance alone. Concept-grounded vaccine detection and the out-of-context media paper handle mixed image-text claims by exposing visual, rhetorical, entity, and caption clues. EmeraldApp and CiteLLM move the same idea into claims about sustainability and scholarship, where the task is to ground a polished sentence in trusted sources rather than accept fluent wording. Chatbot correction and knowledge-graph answer calibration ask when an AI answer should be believed, especially across health, science, politics, or incomplete retrieved evidence. Community Notes, lateral browsing, rhetoric comparison, DREAMS, and misinformation forecasting study the human and social side: how people verify, persuade, rate, engage, and polarize over time. ZK-V, Trustless Feedback, Xemis, decentralized trust layers, video provenance, and agent governance form the infrastructure branch, where the answer is not better wording but verifiable records, privacy-preserving checks, and rules for who can prove what. The deeper move is shared: replace unsupported trust with inspectable evidence.
what_changed: The 2026 version of this family is shaped by generated content and AI-mediated checking becoming ordinary web infrastructure. The evidence shows more work on videos, multimodal social posts, chatbot corrections, agentic systems, scholarly references, sustainability claims, and model confidence, not only text rumor detection. Trust is also moving from after-the-fact classification toward provenance, calibration, governance, and private verification. Several papers treat speed and deployment pressure as central: lightweight out-of-context detection, real-time recommendation trust, in-browser agent execution, edge video provenance, and low-overhead cryptographic receipts. Another change is that human trust is treated as dynamic. Community ratings, lateral browsing behavior, persuasion style, engagement sequences, and polarization signals all matter because the same claim can be accepted, rejected, or revived depending on context and timing.
limits: These papers depend on assumptions the input evidence cannot fully prove. Retrieved evidence must be relevant and not itself misleading. Concept features must capture the cues that actually matter, not just the cues that are easy to name. Crowd ratings and behavioral studies may change across platforms, topics, languages, and political climates. Cryptographic and decentralized systems can prove that a rule was followed, but they do not prove that the original rule, sensor, or human label was correct. Agent-based checkers can still inherit mistakes from their tools or retrieved sources. Confidence estimation helps only if its structural signals track real uncertainty. The evidence reports problems, approaches, and selected gains; it does not show long-term performance under coordinated manipulation, new media formats, legal pressure, or changing incentives.
